storm.summary_layperson: No thunderstorm risk through this window — expect dry conditions with increasing clouds; a slight (30%) chance of scattered storms develops after 5 PM, right as the window ends, with no special local buffering or boosting from the Sound today.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sound water (75°F) and air temperature (75°F) are essentially equal today, so there's no marine layer either protecting the cove from storms or fueling them.
storm.detail_html:
The National Weather Service's Upton, NY office (OKX) is flagging increasing thunderstorm chances late today, with model soundings showing modest instability — 500–1000 J/kg MUCAPE — combined with meaningful 0–6 km wind shear around 32 kt from the WSW. Shear that strong paired with even modest CAPE is enough for the forecaster to write "cannot rule out a severe thunderstorm this afternoon," though the official forecast keeps precipitation chances at 30%, arriving after 5 PM.

Long Island Sound's cooler water normally creates a stabilizing marine layer near the coast that can weaken or delay storms approaching the cove — that's the Sound effect this page usually watches for. Today it isn't a factor: water and air temperature are both sitting right around 75°F (a 0.2°F air–water difference), too close for any meaningful stable layer to form. Call today's local effect neutral, not protective.

For the 11 AM–5 PM window itself, radar shows no cells anywhere near the cove and there are no active NWS alerts, so risk stays low across the full period. The forecast's storm chance sits right at the window's closing bell — after 5 PM — so the window should stay dry from start to finish, with the small evening storm chance arriving just as this window closes.

What would change the call: if afternoon heating pushes CAPE past roughly 1500 J/kg, or radar starts showing cells forming to the west/northwest, risk would step up to moderate quickly given the shear that's already in place — worth a radar recheck heading into the late afternoon and evening.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light gradient wind — no sea breeze today — holds SE around 8–11 kt through the window, with cleaner pressure on the west side of the course in the lee of Tod's Point. Start mid-line and favor the west side; don't expect much shift to play.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today is not a sea-breeze day. The inland/coast air–water temperature gap (deltaT) is only 0.2°F, far under the roughly 5°F needed to build a thermal, and the sea-breeze ensemble confirms it isn't active — only 57% of coastal stations are reading southerly, well short of a building thermal signature. That makes today gradient-only, and since the synoptic gradient itself is light (ensemble mean authoritative wind around 5.6 kt), it's specifically a light gradient wind day: no sea breeze, no afternoon build to look for.

Direction and speed through the window: the model has wind in the SSE–SE band (134°–166°) through the morning and into early afternoon, gradually filling from around 7–8 kt at 11 AM to about 11 kt by 2 PM. Direct model coverage runs out around 2 PM on this forecast cycle; the 3 PM–5 PM values in the table are trend-extrapolated, holding the SE direction and roughly 10–11 kt, since there's no thermal mechanism to either build or collapse the wind through the afternoon.

Where pressure sits: SE flow gets partial shelter from Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) on the east shore of the cove mouth, so pressure and cleaner air favor the west side of the course (Belle Haven/Field Point side); expect the east side, closer to the Point, to be lighter and shiftier.

Shift character: with direction agreement at 0.79 and no thermal in play, expect a fairly persistent SE direction rather than the tactical oscillations you'd get on a mature sea-breeze day — this isn't a tack-on-every-header day, just sail the average and lean west for pressure.

Fleet impact: 8–11 kt sits squarely in the one-design dinghy sweet spot — good, straightforward racing. No postponement risk, and it's not light enough to turn into a drifter either.
